For the record, @garethbowen had previously mentioned that functionality from https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/8681 might prove useful for actually addressing this ticket.  I just wanted to note here that after a cursory review of the code in question, I think that now it should be trivial to add support for toggling off the checking of duplicate phone number on a per-field basis (based on configuration provided in the xform).  

In https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/8681, we added support to the CHT api server for _dynamically_ loading custom data values from xform instance xml elements in the `cht:` namespace.  This is currently being used by the new implementation of the [countdown-timer](https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/apps/reference/forms/app/#countdown-timer) to load the default duration for the timer from the custom `instance::cht:duration` column in the xlsxform.  However, the server code was intentionally written to be generic such that it will load any value from a `instance::cht:###` column into a corresponding HTML attribute (e.g. `data-cht-###`) on the generated element for the form field in question.

This means that, if I am correct, we could just have a custom xlsxform column that could be set to toggle off the dup-checking.  Then, in the [phone widget code](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/814ed5cd488d783784959e60c4066a665319accb/webapp/src/js/enketo/widgets/phone-widget.js), we would just check for the attribute value in the widget constructor and set a flag that would toggle of f the dup checking in the `tel.validate` function.  

---

Unfortunately, I do not have the same confidence that this custom attribute functionality will provide a simple way to improve the validation message that is shown when the field fails validation.  (So, there would still be no good way to provide different messages for invalid vs duplicate numbers if you have both checks enabled.)

- Rework the state managed in webapp to somehow also track the type of the contact in context (or at least track if it is a person or place)  
- Add a `contact` endpoint for getting data for a generic contact.
- Add an endpoint just for checking the _type_ of a contact for a particular id (e.g.`api/v1/entity/${id}/type`) - not great since this still would have to load the doc from the DB to get the type, but not the worst since we are just getting by id.  

Any thoughts here?  Am I missing something?

Met with @garethbowen and @m5r today to discuss https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/9065#issuecomment-2166842427.  The primary conclusions included:

- Our current authorization check with the `can_view_contacts` permission is insufficient.  An _offline_ user with the `can_view_contacts` permission should only be able to view the contacts _they are allowed to replicate._  However, our current implementation of the `person` endpoint is not checking if the user has replication access to the contact they are trying to view.  
  - For the sake of simplicity right now (and to avoid unintentionally leaving any other security loopholes) we should block offline users from accessing the new endpoint. Only online/admin users should be able to call it.  This should not result in a reduction of the intended functionality since offline users in webapp should always be using the local data context anyways and not trying to call though via the remote context.
  - Also, just want to acknowledge that this is conceptually related to [limited online user access](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/7496).  We are not going to try to solve that problem now.
- With the current CHT data model, we often have a uuid of a _contact_, but do not know if that contact is a _person_ or a _place_.  Because of this, we need to support a `contact` endpoint that can be used for reading a generic contact. We can also continue to have `person` and `place` endpoints that can be used for getting guaranteed specific types of contacts.
- Finally, we concluded that we ultimately should also support getting a generic entity ("Doc") by uuid. While this may be undesirable from an encapsulation perspective, it will be incredibly useful as a stop-gap solution for a number of workflows. (Better to make a compromise so that our API is actually usable vs having a conceptually pure API that only covers 80% of the needed workflows...)

Of these conclusions, I think that the only one that needs to be address _in this issue_ is the first.

70% is almost too good to believe. Are you confident in this number? Is it possible some of the other changes you made to this branch are causing it? Is there any other explanation you can think of that might explain this?

> determining how to transition existing users from the old adapter to the new one

The easiest way I can think of is to have _new_ users use the new adapter and existing users continue to use the old adapter. I like this because...

1. It means if there are any undetected issues we can pick them up as it gradually rolls out, rather than disrupting thousands of users in one go. This was useful in transitioning from crosswalk to webview in android.
2. It isn't disruptive to existing users at all. The migration for a user with loads of docs may take some time when they are just trying to do their job. Furthermore the naive implementation would involve duplicating the data, which risks running of out disk space.
3. Users are already being told to sync and wipe and reload their app if they find it slow, so migration of existing users will slowly happen.
4. We can provide either manual migration via a button, or automatic migration at a later date.

There is a complexity cost to this but the way PouchDB is architected it's not a big cost.

I've played around with a variety of options, and nothing is perfect. Basically monorepos work fine for webapps where the distributed code is bundled/compiled but as far as I can see nobody is doing monorepos for node services.

These are my findings...

## 1. Status quo

Each of api, sentinel, webapp, admin, and all shared-libs have their own dependencies and have to be managed separately. This is proven and works ok, but is a pain for updating dependencies, completely incompatible with dependabot, and easy to get dependencies out of sync. It also requires a bunch of complex custom code to piece it together because we're pushing npm out of its comfort zone.

## 2. npm pack in each service

WIP: https://github.com/medic/cht-core/compare/9106-move-dependencies-to-root

I investigated using `bundledDependencies` in api and sentinel to instruct `npm pack` to bundle them into a package that could be extracted into the Docker image. This was really pushing npm to do what we needed, but ultimately there was no way to hoist the version in the root package.json up to each service which meant it didn't solve the problem. There would be a way to do it with custom code generating the package.json but the amount of hackery I needed just to get this to work made it clear it's not a good approach.

## 3. Bundle node services

Seeing as bundling works so well for webapp monorepos, why not just bundle or compile the node services too?

Firstly I looked into using TypeScript which has other advantages for developers but it really didn't want to help me solve the npm issue. Essentially it expected the node modules to still be there when run in production rather than inlining or moving the code it needed. This meant it didn't actually solve the root problem, but maybe I missed an option.

Secondly I looked into using webpack to bundle everything together but as the bundles are not designed to run in node it was also pushing the tool too far past where it wanted to be. It would have probably worked but needed a lot of custom code. I didn't spend too much time on this because it would also produce code that's much harder to debug, so the downside outweighed the potential benefit here.

## 4. npm pack at root

WIP: https://github.com/medic/cht-core/compare/9106-just-share-node-modules

This option involves moving all dependencies for api, sentinel, and shared-libs to the root level, and the using `npm pack` to generate an archive, which can then be extracted into each Docker image. One downside is you end up with more node_modules than you need in the image, but the status quo already has that issue.

Overall this is my preferred approach as it solves the dependencies issue for node services, leaving bundling to solve the issue for webapps, and ultimately means there shouldn't be double ups with, for example, momentjs being defined as a dependency in multiple package.json files and therefore difficult to keep up to date and in sync.

I've found arguments for both sides of dependency management in monorepo: [few dependencies in the root/install dependencies where they're used](https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/managing-dependencies#best-practices-for-dependency-installation) versus [put everything in the root](https://nx.dev/concepts/decisions/dependency-management#single-version-policy)

Looking at the pros/cons, I tend to agree with moving all the dependencies to the root package.json as they get easier to manage and minimizes the risks of having dependency version mismatch. I also remember running into this weird situation when upgrading angular in `webapp` where the angular migration CLI needed to be in the `webapp` directory but relied on dependencies installed in the root `package.json` and I had to temporarily tweak webapp's `package.json` for the CLI to move forward with the migration :man_facepalming: 

This brings up a couple of points:
- how do we make sure we don't keep dragging unused dependencies? we could add tools like [depcheck](https://github.com/depcheck/depcheck) in our CI checks, if we go with a monorepo tool like [Nx](https://nx.dev) it should come with [that feature](https://nx.dev/nx-api/eslint-plugin/documents/dependency-checks) baked in
- how is it going to impact each service's docker image size? can we somehow prune the unused packages from `node_modules`?
- the general consensus seems to be that package managers alone are not enough to manage monorepos ([npm](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/using-npm/workspaces), [pnpm](https://pnpm.io/workspaces), [yarn](https://yarnpkg.com/features/workspaces)) - I haven't dug too deep on this topic yet but there are a couple of well-established solutions out there to help managing monorepos like [Lerna](https://lerna.js.org/), [Nx](https://nx.dev/), [Turborepo](https://turbo.build/repo/docs), [Rush](https://rushjs.io/)
- correct me if I'm wrong but I believe we don't need to do this `npm pack` gymnastic and can rely on [Node's module resolution](https://nodejs.org/api/modules.html#loading-from-node_modules-folders) to import a module from the root `node_modules`

> how is it going to impact each service's docker image size? can we somehow prune the unused packages from node_modules?

That's one of my concerns too. I don't think it'll be a big issue, but will verify before committing to this approach. I'm not _too_ concerned about docker image size because it's not downloaded that often, and when it is, it's to a datacentre.

> the general consensus seems to be that package managers alone are not enough to manage monorepos

I'm quite familiar with Lerna (that's what PouchDB uses) but we seem to be doing so much that's unusual (shared-libs which aren't published to npm, node services, _and_ webapps) that it would struggle. I agree npm isn't enough on its own which is why most of these solutions include custom code, essentially doing what monorepo services would do, but customised to our strange set of requirements.

> correct me if I'm wrong but I believe we don't need to do this npm pack gymnastic

There's not much gymnastics but we could remove it. The key (not yet added to the branch) is to install just the production dependencies and not the devDependencies because the root level has a whole lot of those we don't want to distribute in the image.

@garethbowen I have finally completed a deep dive into this functionality and would appreciate your feedback on this proposed tech design:

### Allow validating number without checking for duplicates

We can add a column to the xlsxform (e.g. `instance::cht:tel_allow_dupe`) that, when populated with `true`  in a `tel` row, would trigger the phone widget to not run the duplicate checking.	(I am not super happy with the column name, so interested in suggestions!)

Currently in the phone widget we are [extending the enketo `types`](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/814ed5cd488d783784959e60c4066a665319accb/webapp/src/js/enketo/widgets/phone-widget.js#L9) object to include a `tel` type with our own custom validation. My proposal is that we add a second `tel_allow_dupe` object to the `types` with a `validate` function that does not run the dupe check. Then during the construction of the phone widget we can check the `data-cht-tel_allow_dup` attribute value (coming from the xlsxform) and if it is set, we update the input's `data-type-xml` to be `tel_allow_dup`.  That will trigger the Enketo logic to use our new `type` to validate the input. This will allow for configuring the dupe checking on a field-by-field basis within each form.

### Allow displaying separate constraint messages when checking both validity and duplication

The main challenge when it comes to displaying separate constraint messages for invalid numbers vs duplicate numbers is actually figuring out how to get the separate internationalized messages to display.  Trying to cram multiple translations into the same xlsxform cell is going to be messy. Having custom columns for each of the localized messages could be possible (e.g. `instance::cht:tel_dupe_msg_en` vs `instance::cht:tel_dupe_msg_es`) but would definitely result in a lot of columns even with just a couple of languages to support (need to have localized versions of both the dupe message and the invalid number message).

Instead, I propose that we take advantage of the fact that we are operating with custom widget code and just load the translated strings from the CHT translation files via the `window.CHTCore.Translate` service.  My assumption is that generic messages for both duplicate and invalid phone numbers would be sufficient for *all forms* and do not really need to be customizable *at the field level*.   This would give a better out-of-the-box experience since we can ship default translations for the messages and partners would not need to mess with `constraint_message` values for `tel` fields in their forms. (But could still customize the generic translated messages if they wanted.)

Functionally, the way I think we should dynamically *choose* which of the messages to display is by using a `MutationObserver` to watch the question element for the `invalid-constraint` class to be added (which Enketo does when it detects a constraint violation).  Adding that class to the question is all that is needed to display the constraint message (which already exists as a hidden `span` on the DOM).  So, when we see the `invalid-constraint`, we can determine which message should be shown and set that onto the `span`.

One challenge here is that the Enekto `validate` call (where we do the initial validity/dupe checking) is completely decoupled and isolated from the widget state (or any other useful context). I have not been able to come up with any feasible way to indicate the result of the `validate` back to the widget.  This means that when we see `invalid-constraint`, we know the validate failed, but we don't know why.  However, this is an exception case (not on the happy path), so a bit of extra processing seems acceptable.  Re-running `phoneNumber.validate` is fine, but running the dupe check query again seems excessive.  Instead, I think we could keep a global (for the form) Set of duplicate phone number values that have been found (during the `validate` calls). Then when deciding what constraint message to show, we can just check this set instead of re-running the dup  query.

As a part of our custom widget code, we could also fix things so that these error messages show in the form _even if there is no value in the `constraint` column._  Currently, if you are using a `tel` field with no `constraint` value and the `validate` fails, the question will turn red (and the value will be rejected), but no message will be shown to the user (even if there is a message in the `constraint_message` column).  This has led to the "standard practice" of setting `true()` in the `constraint` column on `tel` fields. It would be nice to make this unnecessary!

### Deprecate the `tel` type and add support for `tel` appearance

This is not strictly necessary to get the above functionality to work, but it feels like the appropriate time to do this and should be trivial to achieve!  Currently the phone widget is triggered by using the type `tel` in your xlsxform.  This `tel` type is out of spec (custom to the CHT code). It is partially to blame for our [custom XSL](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/beadf34ecfa71f25efe7e7f29f927b0c21c6a2e6/api/src/xsl/openrosa2html5form.xsl#L191) code and it might also require custom Pyxform handling...

The ODK "recommended" method of accepting phone numbers in a form is [via `string` type fields with the `numbers` appearance](https://docs.getodk.org/form-question-types/#number-text-widget).  Ultimately, `string` fields with the `numbers` appearance get transformed in the form HTML to be `input` elements with `type="tel"` (which is the same result as our custom `tel` fields).  These inputs with `type="tel"` will pop the numeric keyboard when highlighted in a mobile browser.

 I think we should update the widget to also get selected for `string` type fields that have _both_ the `numbers` *and* the `tel`appearances.  This way we can deprecate the `tel` xlsxform type and eventually remove it. For maximum passivity, we could also use this as the determining factor for whether to trigger the new constraint message logic.  For forms still using the old `tel` type, we would only use the `constraint_message` set in the form (and not do any dynamic loading).

---

I have spoken to @garethbowen more about this design and his suggestions and am following up here with conclusions and some additional findings.

A couple of factors understood from additional investigations should greatly reduce the hackiness of supporting dynamic constraint messages:

- Enketo will actually emit an `invalidated` event from the `input` element when the validation fails. So, instead of needing a MutationObserver, we can simply listen to `$input` for `invalidated` events.
- Also, we should be able to actually cache the validation _results_ from the `validate` function calls (instead of just keeping a set of dupe phone numbers).  This will let us avoid doing any weird re-validation when we detect an `invalidated` event. Can just check the cache.
- And regarding clearing the cache and memory leaks, etc, I have confirmed that the phone-widget's `static globalReset` function will get called by the [enketo service `unload` function](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/282faee191a448bbcff8f67baa8b3fc844ef14dc/webapp/src/ts/services/enketo.service.ts#L586).  This `unload` function is called at the end of every form workflow.  _But_ even if something goes weird and the `unload` is not called for a form, the form service will preemptively call `unload` again [the next time a form gets rendered](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/282faee191a448bbcff8f67baa8b3fc844ef14dc/webapp/src/ts/services/form.service.ts#L163).  So, the possibility of leaking a cache between forms seems minimal.

Here is a brief summary of the proposed functionality (as I understand it):

Old `type: tel` fields:

- Checks for valid formatting (no change)
- Prevents dups - no way to disable dup check (no change)

New `appearance: tel` fields:

- Checks for valid formatting
- Allows dups by default - can trigger dupe check by adding `instance::cht:unique_tel: true`

Both:

- The constraint message will default to the message provided in `constraint_message`
	- If no `constraint_message` is provided, and the phone number has invalid formatting or is a dup, will use a message from the server translations that is specific to the issue
		- This is a slight behavior change for the old `type: tel` fields. Previously, a constraint message would only be shown if a `constraint` value was set for the field.  If there was no `constraint`, and the validation/dupe-check failed, the field would turn red and be invalidated, but no message would be shown (even if there was a value for `constraint_message`
). Now, we will show a constraint message when appropriate for the invalid tel regardless of the value in the `constraint` column.

---

They dynamic constraint message logic can be implemented independent of the dup-checking.  https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/7514 already exists and seems to be addressed by the proposed behavior.  

So, my plan is to make 2 separate (but sequential) changesets.  One that addresses https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/6390 by supporting `appearance: tel` and the `unique_tel` column.  Then another to address https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/7514 by making the constraint message dynamic.

For maximum clarity, just copying the design goals from https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/6390

- The constraint message will default to the message provided in constraint_message
  - If no constraint_message is provided, and the phone number has invalid formatting or is a dup, will use a message from the server translations that is specific to the issue
    - This is a slight behavior change for the old type: tel fields. Previously, a constraint message would only be shown if a constraint value was set for the field. If there was no constraint, and the validation/dupe-check failed, the field would turn red and be invalidated, but no message would be shown (even if there was a value for constraint_message). Now, we will show a constraint message when appropriate for the invalid tel regardless of the value in the constraint column.

I've done some research over the last few days with a relatively large dataset to give us an idea of how much disk space we could save for large instances. I've generated 5.94M contacts and 840k reports with the [test data generator](https://github.com/medic/test-data-generator) that amounts to a 5.1GB `medic` database and an 18GB `medic-client`. For comparisons, one of our largest deployments has 29.3M documents in the `medic` database that amounts to 80GB and a 187GB `medic-client`.

NB: when measuring the `medic-client` ddoc, I'm looking at the data size on disk that CouchDB returns when querying `GET /medic/_design/medic-client/_info`.

_mrjones sez:_

> You can see check this amount with `curl` and `jq`.  I loaded the data up using the comment below and confirm (but I get 15GB instead of 18!?)
> ```
> curl -qs http://admin:groot@localhost:5984/medic/_design/medic-client/_info | jq '(.view_index.sizes.file/1000/1000/10|round/100)'
> 15.19
> ```


In [this PR](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/pull/9308/files) I managed to shrink `medic-client` from 18GB to 10.2GB so roughly -43%. With similar proportions, that would save about 80GB of storage on that large deployment I mentioned earlier. This is very much napkin math to get an idea of what to expect but it doesn't look as big of a shrink as I initially thought :sweat_smile: 
In my opinion, it's still a win but before moving forward we should see how these views are queried in production and understand the intention behind those queries to figure out what are the expected results. With that piece of info we can better adjust what the view indexes and make sure we reduce the chance of potentially shipping a breaking change in the search behavior.

NB2: The PR doesn't pass CI because some integration and e2e tests are failing. They're few but they rely on the fulltext views to index every field of every documents, they query arbitrary fields and expect the values on those fields to get picked up by the index and have those documents turn up in the search. But basic searches work as expected and their respective tests pass :green_circle: 

Out of curiosity I deleted the 3 `_fulltext` views and measured again, this time `medic-client` went down to 6.2GB. So those 3 fulltext views account for roughly 2/3rd of the size of `medic-client`. Triggering the [view cleanup](https://docs.couchdb.org/en/stable/maintenance/compaction.html#views-cleanup) didn't make any visible difference.

What to do next:
- look at production logs to see how it's used to adjust the view indexing with users' usage and expectations
- decide if it's the right thing to pursue considering the amount of disk space estimated to save
- reproduce the experiment on production data by:
  - cloning a large production instance
  - measuring disk space (on the machine with `df` for example, and via couch APIs)
  - applying desired changes to the `_freetext` views
  - :exclamation::exclamation:  measuring how long it takes for couch to re-index the views
  - and finally measuring how much disk space we saved
- look for other approaches to reduce hosting costs:
  - reduce the size of other ddocs, for reference, on that large deployment I mentioned earlier, `medic-scripts` represents 21.9GB, `medic-conflicts` 32.7GB, `medic-admin` 6.3GB, and `medic` (the ddoc) 34.7GB
  - find a more storage-effective way to do fulltext search (I'm not very convinced we can achieve something meaningful here, client-side search fulltext search in general is not easy)
  - find any other low hanging fruit to reduce RAM/CPU requirements (upgrading couch, optimizing a costly algorithm, that kind of thing...)

volumes:

services:

Okay, after digging into this more, @mrjones-plip and I were able to reproduce the behavior with the simple form I described above (by re-scanning the same barcode).  We found the issue is that the `health_card_id` field gets the value from `SCAN_RESULT`, but this value update is only triggered if the value stored in `SCAN_RESULT` _changes_.  So, if I open the form and scan the value `1234`, this value gets set for `SCAN_RESULT` and the xform logic will update any expressions that depend on `SCAN_RESULT` to reflect this value.  This means that `health_card_id` will get set to `1234`.  _However_ if the user goes and manually edits `health_card_id` to be `""` (or anything else), the value for `health_card_id` will change, but not the value for `SCAN_RESULT`. `SCAN_RESULT` will still be `1234`.  Then, when the user re-scans the barcode with the value `1234`, the xform's logic knows that the value for `SCAN_RESULT` did not change, and so it does not trigger an update to any of the dependent expressions. This is why `health_card_id` does not get updated back to `1234`.  

The most simple and clean way to avoid this problem is to update the form so that the `SCAN_RESULT` field is the one shown to the user for editing.  Then, the `heath_card_id` can be a `calculate` to save the value wherever it actually needs to be in the data hierarchy.  This keeps the _update flow_ of the data linear and avoids any kind of circular dependencies between the `SCAN_RESULT` and `health_card_id` fields.

type | name | label::en | hint | appearance | readonly | default | calculation
-- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | --
begin_group | qr_code | Capturing data from a QR code |   | field-list |   |   |  
begin_group | qr_code_app | NO_LABEL |   | android-app-launcher |   |   |  
string | action | NO_LABEL |   | hidden |   | com.google.zxing.client.android.SCAN |  
begin_group | qr_code_app_outputs | NO_LABEL |   | android-app-outputs |   |   |  
string | SCAN_RESULT | Health card ID | Health card ID should be a 12 digit number | number |   |   |  
end_group | qr_code_app_outputs |   |   |   |   |   |  
end_group | qr_code_app |   |   |   |   |   |  
calculate | health_card_id |   |   |   |   |   | ../qr_code_app/qr_code_app_outputs/SCAN_RESULT
end_group | qr_code |   |   |   |   |   |  

With this new form structure, the user is able to update/clear the health card id value and then re-scan the same QR code as before.

[Screencast from 2024-08-16 10-02-46.webm](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5923a257-31fc-4e33-9cfd-4e3a914a3648)

It is a best practice to keep the data update flow as simple and linear as possible. That being said, this is not always possible for extra complex cases.  The ODK spec does support the concept of a `trigger` column that I think could possibly be useful in cases similar to this.  Unfortunately, we [do not support `trigger` yet](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/8336) in the CHT.

Okay, so, based on [this forum post](https://forum.communityhealthtoolkit.org/t/current-user-data-hydration-with-db-object-issue-using-cht4/3880/4), I have identified a new wrinkle to this issue.  :sweat:   If you look at my original sample form above, you can see that I am trying to load the parent data _in a separate `my_parent_data` group_ contained in the `inputs` group.  This behavior has not been observed to work in any CHT version (as previously noted).  

_However,_ using the contact selector to load contact data for an id value _in its current group_ within the `inputs` did actually work prior to `4.6.0`, but now does not work in `4.6.0+`.  Take the following form for example:

type | name | label::en | appearance | relevant
-- | -- | -- | -- | --
begin_group | inputs |   |   | false()
begin_group | user | NO_LABEL |   |  
db:person | contact_id | User’s Contact | db-object |  
string | role | User’s Role |   |  
end_group | user |   |   |  
end_group |   |   |   |  
note | my_note | User’s Role: ${role} |   |  

I have confirmed that this form will display the `role` value from the user's contact document on `3.17` and on `4.5`, but it will not display the value on `4.6+`.  

The important factors here are the `inputs` group which has special logic around it, and the fact that `inputs` is non-relevant.  Based on my debugging, this issue is actually not technically specific to the contact selector functionality.  The root problem seems to be that updates to form model data in a non-relevant `inputs` group are not actually persisted.  The db-object widget is getting triggered as expected and it is "setting" the proper value onto the `role` field in the form model, but that value is not actually getting stored into the model.  I expect this is because we missed patching something in the setVal logic around `inputs` when it is non-relevant.  :disappointed: 

---

To workaround this issue, you can just move your contact selector group out of the `inputs` group.  You can still reference `inputs` fields, but just do not use the contact selector, itself, inside of `inputs`.

Unfortunately, because of https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/8226 you cannot just create a hidden top-level group for loading the contact data since that will result in a blank page being shown in the form.  But, you can nest the hidden group into the group for an existing page.  This should work on any 3.x-4.x version of the CHT.

type | name | label::en | appearance | relevant | calculation
-- | -- | -- | -- | -- | --
begin_group | inputs |   |   | false() |  
begin_group | user | NO_LABEL |   |   |  
string | contact_id | User’s Contact |   |   |  
end_group | user |   |   |   |  
end_group |   |   |   |   |  
begin_group | my_page | NO_LABEL | field-list |   |  
begin_group | user_contact | NO_LABEL | hidden  |   |  
db:person | _id | User contact Id | db-object |   | ${contact_id}
string | role | User Role | |   |  
end_group |   |   |   |   |  
note | my_note | User’s Role: ${role} |   |   |  
end_group | my_page |   |   |   |

Hi @binokaryg , as we discussed, we'll make only the recipient configurable for now and the message can be constructed so as to match to either recipient. If that also feels strict requirement in the future, we can address that. For now, we'll make recipient accept arrays of input and CHT will try to resolve them in order. 

So the schedule can be configured like:

```json
{
  "group": 2,
  "offset": "105 days",
  "send_time": "07:00 +05:45",
  "recipient": ["patient.phone", "g40_clinic", "g30_health_center"]
}
```

For this schedule, CHT will send the message to `patient.phone`. If that doesn't exist, it'll try to send to `g40_clinic`, if that also doesn't exist, it will try to send to `g30_health_center`.

Just a few design notes here if anyone want to give a PR a shot:

Currently, attachments are added to the Couch document by the EnketoService [in the `xmlToDocs` method](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/69018ea93ca5ce5bead925afa81852e595e7f188/webapp/src/ts/services/enketo.service.ts#L482). However, this method is only called when saving reports (via the `EnketoService.completeNewReport/completeExistingReport` methods). 

Contact forms are saved via the [`ContactSaveService.save` method](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/69018ea93ca5ce5bead925afa81852e595e7f188/webapp/src/ts/services/contact-save.service.ts#L148), which does not currently have any logic to handle attachments. 

We should be able to reuse the same basic attachment processing logic from `xmlToDocs` in the contact save flow. The tricky part is going to be handling the fact that contact forms can create multiple documents (primary doc, sibling docs, repeated child docs), and ensuring that attachments are mapped to the correct document. I think, for each file attachment we will need to look up where in the XML structure it came from, and then map that to the corresponding document. Because of this, I am not sure if there is anything we can easily reuse from `xmlToDocs` directly, but we can at least borrow the logic for processing FileManager files and binary fields to use in our logic that can be added to `ContactSaveService.prepareSubmittedDocsForSave`.

Crazy timing!  I have just been trying to chase down why [PR for refactoring the target aggregate data flow](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/pull/10432) was suddenly breaking the Nepali language tests....

It is definitely because of this.  I did some debugging here and confirmed that when you change the language in the CHT, the LanguageService [sets the `moment` locale](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/da5fe7f731303c6f69315b3992455125f539f91a/webapp/src/ts/services/language.service.ts#L71).  This locale gets used by default for all interactions with `moment` throughout the webapp code base (including in the lines you linked to in the TargetAggregatesService).  _However_, this locale does not get applied to the instance of `moment` used in the rules-engine shared-lib [when it calculates the target doc Id](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/a0334f9de6338536e7a1157b76a9a604733d5942/shared-libs/rules-engine/src/provider-wireup.js#L286).  

So, the target docs always get written with the default (`en`) locale date, but when queried in the TargetAggregateService we are not currently adjusting the locale of the date we use (when the user has configured something besides `en`).  I think the fix here is pretty simple (just set the locale to `en` when getting the interval tag in the TargetAggregateService.

I will include this change in my PR and that should resolve this issue. 👍

Based on my repo archeology, I think this bug has always existed in the target aggregate logic.  The LanguageService has been updating the moment locale [since `2.7.0`](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/commit/28959cdb286ed72b1c7681ba428cc780e10d37dc).  The [original version of the TargetAggregatesService](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/commit/e4240a64265c3b028ee8040961a020ce1588c4cf#diff-808cc486d74c97b0867ac685d8cf1da9792339f777b5fd2a070d9129f721399aR31) (from `3.9.0`) uses basically the same logic for calculating the interval tag with moment.

> Currently, if an SSO/OIDC session expires while offline, the CHT redirects to the Identity Provider (IdP) login page. Since there is no internet, the clinician is locked out of the app

This behavior is unexpected on several levels. 

Once a user has logged in via SSO, their _CHT session_ should not expire until their CouchDB cookie expires.  This should happen [one year after their last request](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/5f59e9f836009c2e6e58b67a59ac4c967935ae9b/couchdb/10-docker-default.ini#L28).  So long as the user has a valid CouchDB session cookie, the CHT should never redirect back to the IdP.  

Secondly, the CHT app should never automatically trigger a user to be logged out when offline (e.g. when not able to communicate to the CHT server).  Even if a user's cookie expires (when they have been offline for 1+ year), the app should still continue to function as expected while offline. It is only when the app comes back online and connects to the server to try and sync that a re-login will be required due to the expired cookie (but once again, this should only happen when the user has been offline for 1+ year).

---

I have been trying to think of possible theories to explain this behavior.  How do you know the SSO/OIDC session is expiring? Are they totally offline or just somewhere with sparse connectivity?  Is this happening for all SSO users or just some?

Are there multiple people using the same device and they are manually logging out and trying to log back in?

Are you using a custom value [for `couch_httpd_auth.timeout`](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/5f59e9f836009c2e6e58b67a59ac4c967935ae9b/couchdb/10-docker-default.ini#L28)?  

> Offline Token Persistence: Securely store OIDC refresh tokens/sessions locally.

This should not be necessary because the CHT just uses OIDC for the initial _user authentication_. Nothing about the user's OIDC session is stored/maintained on the CHT side.  Once the CHT server completes the initial OIDC auth flow, it issues a CouchDB cookie to the user and from that point on, the user's session should behave exactly like other non-SSO users.

> Does this mean that if the default locale in CHT is set to Nepali, it will save the target docs with Nepali locale?

Sorry, by "default" I just meant _moment's default locale_ (which is `en`).  The locale moment uses if you never specified one.

I did a bit of checking and confirmed that (at least with the current version of the CHT) when a Nepali user writes a new target doc it is getting written with the `en` date and not the nepali date (which is actually exactly why the TargetAggregatesService cannot find any target records to aggregate).

About 
> The db-doc functionality in app forms is way more open-ended...
I agree. For contact forms we have at least a modicum of schema we enforce. But for what we are interested in here, each sub-doc ends up with a couchdb document, that may or may not have an attachment. 

When report edit support required the report to have an XML model attachment, only the main document got an xml model. This rendered the sub-docs effectively uneditable. 
Not to mention that editing a report with sub-docs ends up _creating_ new sub-docs instead of editing the existing ones. 

I think sub-doc support, just across the app, is super fragile and seems quite unfinished. 

My sincere hope is that when we introduce chainable forms, we will remove support for sub-doc format.

I tested splitting each view in `medic-client` into its own ddoc on a CHT instance deployed on an EC2 m4.xlarge instance (4 CPUs, 8 GB RAM, and an NVMe EBS volume). The CHT instance had about 500k documents (so not huge), created using the test data generator to produce a mix of contacts, reports, and tasks with realistic hierarchies. This is important when testing views; without realistic data, view indexes are not representative. I also used the test data generator to simulate load. It is hard to be precise about the document creation rate, but I would estimate it to be high for a realistic server, but not extremely high. I first tested using the views as they currently exist in 5.0, and then tested again with each `medic-client` view placed in its own ddoc. Initially, I measured the response time of the `get-ids` endpoint. This did not show any difference between a single ddoc versus one ddoc per view, but those functional tests were complicated and difficult to interpret. I then repeated the test on a similar instance while measuring lower-level server metrics and the response times of the view endpoints themselves. This test did show a large performance difference between one ddoc and one ddoc per view. The bottleneck was not CPU, but IOPS. With one ddoc containing N views, the indexer reads new documents once and writes N indexes into a single file, performing a single fsync. With N ddocs for N views, the indexer reads new documents N times, writes N indexes to N separate files, and performs N fsyncs. My (and Claude’s) hypothesis is that this multiplication of fsyncs results in significantly higher IOPS for the same number of views. There may also be additional per-ddoc work that scales with the number of ddocs. On the test instance, the higher IOPS was enough to cause the CPUs to spend a significant percentage of time in iowait. High iowait percentages have caused severe performance issues in production CHT instances in the past, so this would be very likely to cause unacceptable performance problems for other CHT instances as well. CPU and IO metrics for a single ddoc: And for one ddoc per view: However, one ddoc per view is an extreme case. An alternative would be to split the `medic` and `medic-client` ddocs into several smaller ddocs. With a small enough number, individual reindexing tasks would still be reduced in size, while the increase in IOPS might remain acceptable. Then the question is, what is the best number of ddocs to balance between higher IOPS and smaller reindexing? I would estimate 6-10 based on these results, but that is a guess. And what criteria to use to assign views to the new smaller ddocs?

The issue was, you guessed it, with cache :D 

I was caching local ddoc definitions, but those were also called when the new install was saved, which ended up mutating my cache with adding the :staged: prefix. The problem disappeared on restart because the "install" code doesn't run on every restart, only when the version changes. 

I fixed it by always sending a deep copy of the cached result for other code to play with.

I appreciate the deep analysis @witash . The high IOPS was my main concern and this is hinted in [the CouchDb docs](https://docs.couchdb.org/en/stable/ddocs/views/intro.html#one-vs-multiple-design-documents) as well, although they mention CPU not IOPS. 

> balance between higher IOPS and smaller reindexing

Indeed it is a guess and I think it depends on the instance traffic and storage type. I expect instances with slower storage to hurt more on high write volume. incidentally we have seen large instances opt for slower disks for cost concerns. 

I think we should think of ddocs like database shards, and try to keep ddoc size as balanced as possible. So we don't end up having one ddoc that is massively larger than another. Because the doc distribution, and hence the view size, would be largely dependent on the data set, I don't think there will be a one-size-fits-all kind of deal. I think in the end we'll just roll a dice and commit to a value. 

> And what criteria to use to assign views to the new smaller ddocs?

My preference here would be to split them by "workflow" (as in: areas of the app the use certain views). 
In the old CouchDb days, ddocs would only get indexed if they were explicitly called. That would have rendered an inactive ddoc permanently stale if it was unused, thus saving disk space. In newer versions, ddocs are [indexed in the background](https://docs.couchdb.org/en/stable/config/indexbuilds.html), with an option to disable background indexing for some ddocs. If we are ever to use this background index opt-out for disk space saving, along with a [different view warming upgrade strategy](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/10383), we would need views to be "logically" grouped in order to allow the index to not be required. 

For example: say a project doesn't use SMS or transitions, so then every view for SMS and transitions can be skipped. 
Same for purging. the `medic` ddoc has a view called `tasks_in_terminal_state` that is only used for purging terminal state tasks. if purging is disabled, this view just wastes space. 

I know there would be a lot of tinkering if we were to group views like this, but I would be super happy to help with this.

There's some patterns that emerge
1. we have to keep the distinction between what doesn't get downloaded for offline clients and what does
2. there are several views that are used only by the frontend (found only in webapp/ or shared-libs/search). Some of these seem like they could be more generic and just happen to only be used in the fronted (`contacts_by_place`, `reports_by_place`, `data_records_by_type`), but others seem to be written specifically for some ui element
3. Some views are referenced in many different places and are kind of 'general purpose' (`contacts_by_phone`, `contacts_by_type`).
4. That leaves many otherwise single purpose views that don't group together naturally with any other views (`tasks_in_terminal_state`)

So using these criteria: 
1. keeping the distinction between what doesn't get downloaded for offline clients and what does
2. separating client only, shared, and server only (server includes sentinel and api)
3. separating server only views (current medic) by function, not minding a few single view ddocs to avoid a 'miscellaneous' bucket
4. separating client only and shared views by doc type, not minding a few views that don't quite fit to avoid too many single view ddocs
my proposal would be

## auth
Views used for replication and authorization:
- `contacts_by_depth`
- `contacts_by_primary_contact`

## client-contacts
Client-only views that index contacts:
- `contacts_by_last_visited`
- `contacts_by_parent`
- `contacts_by_place`

## client-reports
Client-only views that index reports (and messages):
- `data_records_by_type`
- `messages_by_contact_date`
- `reports_by_place`
- `reports_by_validity`
- `reports_by_verification`
- `visits_by_date`

## shared-contacts
General-purpose views related to contacts:
- `contacts_by_phone`
- `contacts_by_reference`
- `contacts_by_type`
- `registered_patients` — does not quite belong; seems old and is only in `shared` because of transitions
- `tasks_by_contact` — does not quite belong

## shared-reports
General-purpose views related to reports:
- `reports_by_date`
- `reports_by_form`
- `reports_by_subject`

## shared-docs
General-purpose views. Although they all have “doc” in the name, they do not have much else in common:
- `doc_by_type`
- `docs_by_id_lineage`
- `docs_by_shortcode`

## doc-summaries
Special case that gets its own ddoc. It is only used for online users; offline users calculate summaries:
- `doc-summaries-by-id`

## purging
The only view related to purging:
- `tasks_in_terminal_state`

## report-transitions
Three related views that seem to be used only in transitions and may not be relevant for all deployments:
- `reports_by_form_and_parent`
- `reports_by_form_year_month_parent_reported_date`
- `reports_by_form_year_week_parent_reported_date`

Thanks for putting this together, @mrjones-plip! I appreciate you thinking about contributor visibility.

I have some concerns about this approach that I wanted to share:

- Readability: Adding contributor links inline with each item would make the release notes quite dense. The current format keeps things scannable for readers who just want to know what changed. This would also lead to the same names appearing repeatedly throughout the page, adding visual noise without much added value.
- Attribution completeness: Code authors are only part of the story. Designers, PMs, community managers, and others all contribute to features but wouldn't show up in commit metadata. Highlighting only code contributors could inadvertently diminish the work of everyone else on those features.
- Current approach has merit: The shared code "Contributors" section at the bottom actually reflects something true: releases are a team/community effort. There's value in that collective acknowledgment rather than creating a hierarchy of visibility.

I am not opposed to improving contributor recognition, but I wonder whether there are alternatives that can address your goal without these trade-offs. What problem are you most trying to solve here? Happy to brainstorm other options.

> db admins in later versions of couch do not have the "_admin" role that we were looking for, instead they have an "admin" role or no roles at all.

Something feels a bit off here.  🤔 I have not found any documentation/announcement to suggest this.  The [Couch Security Docs](https://docs.couchdb.org/en/stable/api/database/security.html#db-security) still indicate that the `_admin` role is the reserved system role for DB admins.

I did a bit of testing locally. Spinning up fresh instances for both `4.5.0` and `5.0.0`, I confirmed that the admin `medic` user for both has the `_admin` role (as returned from the Couch `_session` endpoint). If I _add_ a doc in `_users` db, for `org.couchdb.users:medic` with a `roles` array, (e.g. `['admin']), then these roles are _appended_ to the user's roles returned from `_session` (so `"userCtx":{"name":"medic","roles":["_admin", "admin"]}`).  If I create a new user's doc (for a user that is not in the `cluster-credentials.ini`) and give that user the `_admin` role, I get an error:

> Save failed: No system roles (starting with underscore) in users db.

If I add a new user to the `cluster-credentials.ini`, they are automatically assigned the `_admin` role.  

---

Now, of course, "admin" users can be specified at the DB level by adding new roles (or usernames) to the DB's `_security` config. So, it is possible to have a _custom_ `admin` role that has administrator access to the `medic` db, etc.  But, as far as I know we have nothing like this by default in the CHT. So, this would be a custom role and should be configured with the other roles in the app-settings.

Okay, I think I found the root problem.  TLDR I think we accidentally left a [100 result `limit`](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/4d3c72f61a17d761f76bf6efbef3d13bf619f491/shared-libs/cht-datasource/src/libs/core.ts#L210) in the cht-datasource "paged generator" code when it should have been updated to use the [default 10000 result limit](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/4d3c72f61a17d761f76bf6efbef3d13bf619f491/shared-libs/cht-datasource/src/libs/constants.ts#L5) when paging uuids....  This means that when you run a freetext search and there are a lot of results, we will round-trip to the DB for ever 100 uuids that are found by the search.  😬 This does affect both online and offline users (though presumably offline users are less impacted because they have less total search results and no network latency for round-trips to Pouch).

We [set the 10000 result limit](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/4d3c72f61a17d761f76bf6efbef3d13bf619f491/shared-libs/cht-datasource/src/index.ts#L119) as the default when _getting a "page" of uuids_ from cht-datasource. But, shared-libs/search needs to get _all_ uuids matching the freetext search.  So, [its logic](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/4d3c72f61a17d761f76bf6efbef3d13bf619f491/shared-libs/search/src/freetext-query.js#L38) just goes straight into the generator-based function that does "automatic" paging.  And then spins through all results of the generator (behind the scenes the generator is fetching uuids in batches of 100...).  We had to have some kind of paging here because Nouveau [has a default limit of 25](https://docs.couchdb.org/en/stable/ddocs/nouveau.html) if you do not set some other limit.  So, the idea was to just grab 10000 at a time...  😞 

The good news is that I guess this should be easy to fix since we just need to update the `getPagedGenerator` logic to _not_ explicitly set the `limit` value.  I think if we leave off that parameter, then we will just use the default `limit` value defined for the `fetchFunction` and this should give us the desired flexing between the `DEFAULT_DOCS_PAGE_LIMIT` of `100` vs the `DEFAULT_IDS_PAGE_LIMIT` of `10000`....

> Simple freetext search seems to get all results for the search for every search "page" instead of getting one page at a time.

One thing to note (because you called this out in the issue description) is that AFICT the freetext search _has never used db paging_.  Instead, shared-libs/search always used its "manual" paging for freetext search.  Even on the pre-nouveau code (e.g. `4.22.0`) the freetext requests [never have `ordered` set](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/fbf0a0cca4c6eab1471f46a6dea3c6e5ec535f70/shared-libs/search/src/search.js#L97) and so always drop down into the manual pagination process which queries the views without any `limit`.  The difference that was introduced in `5.0.0` was that if your search yields 1000 results, before `5.0.0` we would run one view query with no `limit` and get back all 1000 results and then manually return the first 50 of them.  Now, after `5.0.0` we will end up running _10_ round-trip Nouveau queries (for 100 results each).  Then we combine all the results and manually return the first 50.

Thank you for checking back in on this @jkuester. Before I give an answer in haste, I want to sanity-check my understanding of the different approaches by pitting them against each other. Please correct me where I'm off. This will help me make a more informed call and better contribute to the plugin squad going forward.

| Topic | POC: Bundled plugin libs (this PR) | We-component - config based UI extensions |
|---|---|---|
| Delivery | Supplied as libraries and bundled with the webapp at build time. Higher barrier of entry (image building).  | Supplied via config and uploaded as doc attachments. Familiar usage paradigm, quicker to onboard, simpler project setup. |
| Download model | All users download all plugins. It blurs the line between "core" and "extension". Larger download size. Visibility is largely cosmetic. | Extensions are replicated/downloaded conditionally by role/permission. Additionally, the same runtime routing checks apply as in POC (permission change). Mostly, code that shouldn't exist, won't. | 
| Bundling size | Always increases, regardless of usage. | Only increases for users who actually need the extension | 
| Offline support | Works offline (bundled) | Works offline (replicated like extension libs) |
| UI composition | Preset displays with limited configurability through `app_settings.json`. Onus on CHT to update/extend functionality. Settings loaded at runtime to mutate navigation. Plugin code available on app load. | Open ended display. Onus is on AUTHOR to implement the visuals they're interested in. Opportunity for marketplace. Nav placement declared ahead of time via descriptor (`.properties`). Descriptor loaded at runtime to mutate navigation. Plugin code loaded as necessary. | 
| Load timing | All plugins loaded async on application startup, but still eagerly for all users. | JS loaded only when the extension is needed. |
| Framework constraints | Angular-hosted and Angular-coupled | Angular, vanilla JS, or anything that builds to single JS file. |
| Upgrade coupling | Tightly coupled to CHT Core releases | Extensions can evolve independently of core. Might need some sort of prop to indicate compatibility with core (similar to `engines` prop on `package.json`). |
| Architectural feel | Optional code paths shipped with core | Extensions whose existence and execution can be enforced at delivery time, not just runtime |

From my understanding, the navigation is ultimately mutated by both approaches. The POC favours a grouped nav config approach, whereas the squad proposal favours a per-extension approach. Both will need a doc attachment to be loaded at runtime to set the extension routes. 

Where the approaches meaningfully diverge is what happens after that point. The squad proposal seems way more author friendly and kinder to the client device in terms of resource consumption (upfront vs conditional). There's a box where the extension code is allowed to run in, it shouldn't have access things we don't intentionally expose. Also, seems safer to NOT have unnecessary code hanging around (conditional replication). 

Over and above the technical details, the approaches also differ on ownership. The POC places ongoing responsibility on the CHT team to curate, bundle, and ship plugin code. The squad proposal shifts ownership to the community, to implement/maintain their needs. Core is just a vessel.

to get the sizes of each view in a ddoc, use the couchdb remote shell `remsh` (at `/opt/couchdb/bin/remsh` in the couchdb container:
```erlang
  rr(couch_mrview_util).

  ViewSizes = fun(DbName, DDocId) ->
      lists:foldl(fun(Shard, Acc) ->
          ShardName = mem3:name(Shard),
          {ok, Pid} = couch_index_server:get_index(couch_mrview_index, ShardName, DDocId),
          {ok, St} = couch_index:get_state(Pid, 0),
          lists:foldl(fun(V, A) ->
              Name = case V#mrview.reduce_funs of
                  [] -> hd(V#mrview.map_names);
                  [{N,_}|_] -> N
              end,
              Size = couch_btree:size(V#mrview.btree),
              maps:update_with(Name, fun(S) -> S + Size end, Size, A)
          end, Acc, St#mrst.views)
      end, #{}, mem3:local_shards(DbName))
  end.

```

I think this request makes sense. 👍 Historically the "batch" operations on contacts have been handled by admins via cht-conf commands (like the [delete-contacts](https://github.com/medic/cht-conf/blob/ce26d62ac1d44cfb735a56b7855a7d234ada8b2d/src/fn/delete-contacts.js#L50) action).  However, more and more we have been hearing about the need for users to be able to self-serve these operations from within the app.  (E.g. the `move-contacts` and `merge-contacts` actions are additional ones that are needed.)  

There are a number of technical considerations that come with this functionality, but I think it should definitely be possible to implement it in a way that server-side logic could be triggered by _online_ users.

Regarding @Raam751's questions:
- I would describe CouchDB's delete functionality (which I _think_ is what is used when deleting a contact here from the UI) as a "hard-ish" delete.  The deleted doc will immediately not be available in subsequent requests to the DB. However, previous revisions of the doc remain stored in the DB until they are eventually purged during the periodic database compaction (leaving only a "tombstone" record indicating the doc existing but not containing any of its data).  At this time we have not implemented a true "soft delete" that is reflected on the server (or for online users). However, [CHT purging](https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/technical-overview/data/performance/purging/) is a form of "soft" delete from offline user devices.
- I think the delete button is disabled in the screenshot because the currently selected contact has children (and since we currently do not support cascading deletes, we do not let you delete a parent contact that has children).  That being said, the [can_delete_contacts permission](https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/building/reference/app-settings/user-permissions/) can be used to control exactly which roles have the ability to delete contacts at all.

We cannot upgrade to CouchDb 3.5.1, as it comes with a massive regression in indexing time for Nouveau indexes. I have run our benchmarking script over the new version and there are very concerning performance degradations when it comes to indexing Nouveau. 

For reference these are the [benchmark results for 3.5.0](https://github.com/medic/scalability-results/blob/main/results/10646-add-indexing-benchmark-22101618369/benchmark_results.md#nouveau_index-benchmark) and these are the [benchmark results for 3.5.1](https://github.com/medic/scalability-results/blob/main/results/copy-of-shashi-couch-upgrade-take-2-22138424173/benchmark_results.md)

| CouchDB Version | 3.5.0 | 3.5.1 | difference |
|--------|--------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------| --|
| Nouveau Indexing Time | 184,828ms (~3.1 min) | 2,761,777ms (~46 min) | +1395% slower |
| _changes (10k limit, worst) | 1,982ms | 3,026ms | +52.7% slower |
| _all_docs (10k limit, worst) | 1,607ms | 3,603ms | +124% slower |

Discussing with the CouchDb team, this seems to be related to switching [Nouveau to using http2](https://github.com/apache/couchdb/pull/5598). The CouchDb team have confirmed the performance degradation and will work on a fix, and this fix will be included in a future CouchDb version. 

Closing this in anticipation of Couch 3.5.2.

Support for this approach [is now in chtoolbox](https://github.com/jkuester/chtoolbox/pull/316).  It works and provides good disk space benefits as noted above.

Unfortunately, it is not viable for general use. The main issue is the failure scenario where there is still not enough disk space to re-index the views (even using the `chtx design upgrade` command).  In that scenario, the CHT instance will go down, the current views will be deleted (so the instance cannot be restarted) and then we will try to build the new versions of the views.  If those new views fail to build (because you run out of disk space) then you are stuck. You might not be able to revert back to the old views because you probably will  not have the disk space to re-build those.  At that point the only options for getting the instance back up will be to increase the disk space or restore from backup.

One of the hacks with a side car I was excited about was the ability to "backport" this to pre-CHT 5.2.  I put backport in quotes as I'm envisioning CHT Core would be entirely unaware of the feature.  The sidecar could be added to our existing compose file and reach right into the [couch data volume](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/4bbafb36ae1f42579cdecaeedf725a160a545137/scripts/build/cht-couchdb-single-node.yml.template#L5) and trivially copy it to separate, backup volume.

Another thought I was that the sidecar could actually be two very slim containers:
* one container that reaches into aforementioned couchdb volume and then exposes the couchdb shards to be easily read (backup) or written (restored) to.  I envision a rando port like `4000` that would leverage dead simple protocol like SCP, but could be smart with something like rsync (or even [borg](https://www.borgbackup.org/)?!)). Of course encrypted on the wire and with strong authenticated.
* a second thin container would know the credentials and use the first containers exposed port & protocol to copy the files to a data volume.  

We deploy them both in the same compose file as a happy path.  A happy ++ path is that you deploy the second container on another VM and BAMO!! off VM backup!  OR...a second data center!?  All you need is access to the `4000` port and the credentials and you're good to backup and restore.  There's no reason to not have multiples of the 2nd container running!

Finally, it seems like we only wanted to have the happy path backup the data shards and not the index shards - massive savings on space as we estimate 70-90% of a deployments data is taken up by the indexes.  This, however, seems like an implementation detail where it would be trivial to offer a full backup (opt in, of course) which would play really nice with the second container to be configured slightly differently when space is not at such an optimum.

> That doesn't work in Docker local, because it needs docker swarm to do cross-machine communication Yup yup - agreed! However, that's the trick we can do with the slim "backup server" I have. It goes out of it's way to securely expose a way to backup the files both within the docker network, but just as easily outside the docker network. I've done up a demo below that uses our [production Core CouchDB compose file](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/master/scripts/build/cht-couchdb-single-node.yml.template), but with two extra containers: the `backup-server` and the `backup-client`. Critically, the backup server has `ports: "2222:22"` declared, which expose a backup protocol externally (SSH in this case, but could be what ever we choose). In the first half the demo there's a happy path that just works with no extra config from the user. But then in the second half of the demo, JUST the backup client is spun up on a fully separate machine and all it has is the private key and the address of the backup server. This scales nicely in that the backup client can decide how much to backup (just shards or shards + indexes?) as well as how much retention to have (having only one backup that happily backs up your corrupt shards won't help, where as having 7 days of backups will help immensely). Critically, this solves the problem nicely for a docker based deployment, but to do fully "on another VM" when hosting in k8s would require more setup. This setup could be done with an SSH tunnel sidecar as we've [done for superset](https://github.com/medic/data-system/issues/45#issuecomment-2217689034) or a bastion host as we've [done for CHT Sync](https://github.com/medic/cht-docs/pull/1700). Otherwise, I don't think we should let perfect get in the way of good and if we add this to the 2 sidecars to the helm charts and they just backup within the same infra, this would be a big win. It would be a lot easier to document how to expose a k8s backup server if it's up and running than if it doesn't exist at all 🤷

@raphaelkenyuri thanks for the details here!  👍 One angle of this that has been [previously discussed](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/7284) was around support for some kind of "pin authentication" that could exist as an additional layer on top of the current CHT session.  (Basically the valid session cookies are maintained on the device, but access to the app is gated via a pin code such that the user must enter a pin to be able to open the app.)

Discussing this in the context of https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/10720 is really helpful since I think that will let us find the necessary feature requirements here.  

One of the big things to consider first is if the goal here is _user convenience_ (e.g. just helping users make sure they are entering data with the correct account so the data is consistent) or if you require strong on-device _data security_?  Currently, because the CHT app does not require any kind of authentication when opened (once you have logged in via the server), the CHT data stored on the device _is not encrypted_ (besides any partition-level encryption that exists at the Android system level).  So, if the user has access to an unlocked device, they have access to the CHT data stored on that device.  

Just supporting a "user convenience" pin could be a very simple update to cht-android. In this case, https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/10720 could be implemented in such a way that each user would only see _their own_ data in the app (but, technically, at the file-system level they could still dump the unencrypted data of the other user...). However, if we need to protect the data of one user from being accessed at all by another person with access to the same device, then it is going to require a lot more changes and security considerations.

---

This [forum thread](https://forum.communityhealthtoolkit.org/t/enhancing-security-of-cht-apps-through-two-factor-authentication-2fa/1953) is a previous conversation that we had around similar challenges. It highlights some of the operational difficulties that are inherent to increased data security.

I have added some relevant comments over in https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/10719, but just to directly address a few things here:

These features _technically_ already exist with how the CHT webapp stores data. (Currently, there is just no way _from the UI_ to actually switch between accounts, but the data from different users is already stored distinctly on the device.) So, these features should be trivial to achieve.

- Allow N user accounts to be registered on a device (ideally configurable by deployment administrators)
- Each account should maintain its own locally cached data and credential hash, isolated from other accounts

IMHO these features should be reasonably simple to implement (with due consideration for CHT-auth vs pin-auth as noted in https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/10719):

- Users should be able to switch between accounts from the login screen without requiring internet connectivity, provided they have previously logged in online at least once
- Deployments should be able to cap the number of cached accounts per device to manage storage

This one is where things get tricky....:

- Account data isolation must be enforced: User A must not be able to access User B's cached records

As I noted in my comment on https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/10719, the effort required to implement this all depends on exactly what you mean by "isolation must be enforced".  TLDR it should be easy to make it so that when User B opens the app, they do not see the data from User A.  However, it could be a lot more challenging to make it so that when User B has physical access to the unlocked device, there is no possible why they could ever access any of User A's data (even if they dump the contents of the partition).

When testing staging these ddocs on an EC2 instance with 8GB memory, the instance ran out of memory and had to be restarted.

This was not seen in earlier testing because those tests simulated staging by adding the ddocs manually instead of actually using the cht upgrade. That process is different; when creating a new ddoc, it will be built automatically by the autoindexer "ken", which has a maximum number of active tasks (default 20). When using the cht's staging process, the endpoint for each view is polled, which was necessary to force the index to be 'pre-warmed' in previous couchdb versions that did not include ken. When indexing tasks are triggered by http requests, there is no maximum number; it triggers as many tasks as possible which is the number of shards * the number of ddocs.
This means 56 (9 ddocs * 8 shards) indexing tasks are running, which uses up more memory than expected.
I think mostly because of spidermonkey, the javascript interpreter that runs the map functions.

During load testing, the memory use was less because the indexing tasks were smaller and were not running continuously; they were able to keep up with new updates.

This increase in memory use during staging might mean that the proposed 9 ddocs are still too many.
However, testing a hypothetical 5.x upgrade with the current ddocs, rebuilding just medic and medic-client, had similar memory usage (and the 8GB test instance was not able to finish rebuilding without running out of memory).
So it's a little arbitrary, but I think slightly fewer than 9 ddocs might be a better balance.
But for further testing, I used a 16GB instance instead of 8GB.

Okay, I have spent some time digging in deeper on a design for this. Here is a summary of my current thoughts.

### Complexities
- Moves need to be initiated and completed by offline users.
- The users on either end of the move might not have access to the contact hierarchy for the source/destination.
- Because of `replication_depth` configuration, users might not have complete access to all of a moved contact's child contacts and/or reports.

### Prior Work
- Implementation for this feature can follow similar patterns to what we have done for:
	- [Muting](https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/building/reference/app-settings/transitions/#muting)
	- [Offline User Replace](https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/building/reference/app-settings/transitions/#replace-user)
 
### Ongoing work
- https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/10706 intends to add *server-side* support for advanced contact operations (like moving a contact).  We should leverage this functionality. The main thing this issue needs to resolve is the user-facing workflow (particularly for offline users).

### Different types of moves
- `Pull` - Move inaccessible contact to accessible destination
	- Out of scope for this issue.
- `Push` - Move accessible contact to inaccessible destination
	- The move is initiated by the source user. Somehow the destination user is given the ability to select the `parent` place for the contact to be moved.  Once that is selected, the server does the move.
	- Can "mute" the moved contact on the source user's device.
	- Not a clear way for the source user to choose the destination. May need some bespoke cache of summary data for all the "facilities" (places referenced by the `facility_id` of a user).
	- Not a clear way to notify the destination user.  Somehow we need to "break-the-glass" and allow the contact to replicate to the destination user before finalizing the move (so that we actually have a `parent` value to use).  Might need something similar to [`needs_signoff`](https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/technical-overview/data/performance/replication/#supervisor-signoff) but that activates on the destination facility id that was chosen by the source user.
- `Internal` - Move accessible contact to accessible destination
	- Everything on the device is updated via a client-side transition.
	- Contact is marked as needing the move "finalized" by the server (to make sure any docs the user does not have access to are also updated).

For both `Push` and `Internal` moves we will need some kind of server-side async processing (like a Sentinel transition) that can actually handle updating the contacts/reports (with functionality added in https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/10706)

👍 100%.  And yeah, a "pull" is going to be even more complicated. (Though maybe could have a similar workflow 🤔):

- User A talks to the patient and registers a new contact for them (while offline).  But since the patient mentioned they are actually from Area B, the user marks the contact as needing "merged" with a contact from Area B.
- User A syncs and the contact is uploaded to the server.
- The server "merges" the existing version of the contact (and all related contacts/reports) from Area B to the new one in Area A
  - One tricky thing to sort out here is that this cannot just be a one-time thing. 😓 User B might be offline and have un-uploaded reports for the contact. When User B comes back online, they need to be able to sync those reports (somehow) and then the server will again need to transition them to Area A.

---

Regarding how to pick Areas to push or pull from when the user does not have access to all the other areas, etc, one idea I had for how to operationalize this is to implement https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/9875 so that you can have `select_*` questions in forms that reference an "external" dataset.  Basically I am imagining you could upload a `resource` file which is a CSV of Areas (or whatever users/locations you want to be able to pick from). Then in your "transfer" form, the you do the `select_*_from_file` against that uploaded CSV.  Deployments would still have to upload new versions of that csv as new users/areas are added/removed, but it might be more manageable then having to edit the form all the time....

Great discussion! PIN-based/bio- authentication is a valid approach, though managing PINs across a large pool of shared devices can introduce operational overhead - particularly when enforcing policies around PIN strength and rotation. An alternative worth considering is a credential-hash-based offline re-authentication model:

- On the first successful online login, the CHT Android app creates a salted hash of the user credentials and stores it securely in the local database - not plaintext credentials.
- When offline, if the user attempts to log in again with the same [serverUrl, username] pair that was last authenticated, the Android SDK compares the submitted credentials against the stored hash locally, without any network call. If the hash matches, the user gets access to the locally cached data.
- Offline login is strictly limited to the last authenticated user/server pair. A different user cannot log in offline - they must be online for first-time authentication.
- Account disablement is respected: if the server marks an account as disabled, the local database is wiped on the next successful online sync.
- Logout preserves data but removes credentials, so metadata and data remain on device for the next login.

Critically, offline re-authentication is purely a client-side gate to locally cached data - it does not touch, extend, or bypass the server-side session, meaning server-side security controls remain fully intact.

This approach could complement or replace PIN-based access, particularly in deployments with short session windows and shared devices, as it ties authentication directly to the user's actual credentials rather than a separate PIN they need to remember or manage.

👍 So, an offline credential-hash approach like you have described _could_ probably be implemented within the CHT.  However, I don't think there is any way to do it _in conjunction with the OIDC authentication_.  In fact, one of the key "features" of OIDC authentication is that none of the CHT system (neither the client or the server) every actually has access to any of the user's credentials.  All of the authentication happens with the 3rd-party identity provider and so in the OIDC case, I do not see how the CHT would have anything to hash.  🤔

Here is some more context from related forum threads:
- [Ability to check if a form is previously filled for purged forms](https://forum.communityhealthtoolkit.org/t/ability-to-check-if-a-form-is-previously-filled-for-purged-forms/4565)
- [Setup purge config to always leave the most recent report (per type)](https://forum.communityhealthtoolkit.org/t/setup-purge-config-to-always-leave-the-most-recent-report-per-type/4583)

We need a way to persist some bits of information in CouchDB that should survive purging.

Some examples:
- When was the last assessment done for this patient?
  - so that the user knows whether to prioritize another assessment from action. For example, when they are near the household.
- How many times a woman was pregnant in the past? Were there any danger signs?
  - This is important for longitudinal care. If the past records disappear without any signs, the tool becomes more case-centric rather than person-centric for the end user. It only cares about the current case and forgets about the past cases.
- All-time targets
  - It can be confusing for the users to see the numbers suddenly decrease in the targets counter.
