@mrjones-plip The scope is a bit broader than just `opts.headers.set()` calls. That pattern is specific to the PouchDB fetch plugin, but we have header magic strings in a few other patterns too, like `res.setHeader(...)`, `req.headers[...]`, and object literals.

I did a quick scan and here are the custom/medic specific headers beyond `REQUEST_ID` that I think are worth constantizing:

| Header | Source files |
|---|---|
| `X-Medic-Service` | `api/src/db.js`, `sentinel/src/db.js` |
| `X-Medic-User` | `sentinel/src/db.js`, `api/src/auth.js` |
| `medic-replication-id` | `webapp/src/js/bootstrapper/index.js`, `api/src/middleware/authorization.js` |
| `logout-authorization` | `api/src/server-utils.js`, `webapp/src/ts/app.component.ts` |

There are also standard HTTP headers (`Content-Type`, `Cache-Control`, CORS headers, etc.) floating around, but I'd leave those out of scope here. They're well known strings and constantizing them just adds indirection without much payoff. The real value is in these custom ones that span multiple packages, where a typo would actually be painful to debug.

Hii @kennsippell, @mrjones-plip, @jkuester

I've been looking into this bug and went ahead and raised a PR #10795 for it — fix(#10341): revoke permissions when user role is deleted from app_settings.

The root cause was that all three permission-checking codepaths (cht-datasource, user-management, and the API) were only comparing the user's roles against app_settings.permissions without ever checking if those roles still exist in app_settings.roles. So even after deleting a role, the permissions mappings stayed intact and users kept their access.

The fix filters out any deleted roles before the permission check runs. Kept it backwards compatible — if roles config is empty, no filtering happens.

Would really appreciate a review and any feedback! Happy to make changes if I've missed anything or approached it the wrong way.

Thanks @dianabarsan, you're right that a global queue is too broad.
The race comes from unique() querying before the doc is saved.

I can think of two options:
- Option A (single-pod): Register an in-memory claim keyed on the unique field values before querying CouchDB in validation_utils.js. Since Node.js is single-threaded, any concurrent unique() call with the same fields will find the pending claim and short-circuit as a duplicate. Claim is released after saveDoc().
- Option B (multi-pod): CouchDB-backed lock doc (unique:<hash>) to detect in-flight duplicates across instances.

I prefer Option A as a minimal, non-blocking fix.

Ultimately it seems that _Couch/Pouch view queries,_ themselves, support equivocating between Arabic and Devanagari numerals.  I confirmed this by creating two contacts in my local CouchDB, one with a patient_id of `12346` and one with `१२३४६`.  Then I manually queried `/medic/_design/medic/_view/docs_by_shortcode` (directly against the Couch endpoint without even proxying through CHT). I am not 100% sure what the best fix here is... 🤔 If there is a simple 1-to-1 mapping between Arabic and Devanagari, then it is probably not too crazy to be able to automatically add an `or` to our Lucene search query, but it would be a janky character-by-character thing...  😓 I also see various locales in the [Couch Nouveau Analyzer docs](https://docs.couchdb.org/en/stable/ddocs/nouveau.html#analyzers). — Attachment routing for sub-contacts

To build on @vikrantwiz02  idea - here is the proposed solution

## Problem
In both contact and app forms, every uploaded file is attached to the **main** doc regardless of the sibling (contact) or child doc it was uploaded in.

e.g. if you upload a photo inside a CHW (sibling) form during a health facility creation, the photo is attached to the health facility doc.

This is because the logic that maps the uploaded files to the doc saved to CouchDB short-circuits and maps all attachments to the 'main' doc.

## Proposed approach

Update the mapping logic to correctly route uploaded files to the right doc.

1. **Generate a file xml section look up map** - walk main, sibling, and each of the repeated docs xml to map to already prepared js doc. The doc returned is the one to attach the attachement to.
2. **Route file-widget uploads** - get the file name from `[type=binary]` nodes (file uploads) text value and map it to the it's entry in files uploadd (`FileManager.getCurrentFiles()`). This gives you the file object to attach to the doc returned by the map in 1 above.
3. **Route inline binary blobs** - binary attachments are inlined in the node elements as base64 text e.g draw / signature widgets. the same way — walk from the binary node up to its section root, look up the owning doc, attach.
4. **Per-doc processingc** - replicate the existing sanitization, clean up helpers that are used on the main doc in current implementation to subling and repeated docs.
5. **Validations** - validate attachments size before processing / saving. this already exists  for reports.

## Non functinal requirements
- unit tests to accompany each implementation
- replicate child-contacts implementation to sub reports with consistent validations
- E2E tests covering the feature impelementation

## Out of scope
- bulk editing child doc attachments - editing pulls main doc only; so, no bulk editing of child docs attachments

## Limitations

- ~**Same filenamename** - same file different content causes attachment overwrite.~ Filename have timestamp appended for uniqueness. 
- ~**Sanitized filename collisions after stripping special characters**: inherent in current implementation.~ Filename have timestamp appended for uniqueness. 

## Sub issues

Self-contained sub-issues with own unit tests; the E2E test is a separate final issue so it can assert the full routing picture end-to-end.

1. Wire `validateAttachments` on the contact-save path.
2. Add attachment - doc mapping (`buildAttachmentOwnerIndex`)
3. Route file-widget and inline-binary attachments per-doc using the mapping, with per-doc processing
4. E2E test: parent-registration form with uploads in main, sibling, and repeat sections.

**Analysis:** The flakiness in the should only store 10 history entries is caused by a race condition between the API response and the asynchronous audit-writing process. In routing.js, audit.expressCallback is triggered but not awaited before the response is sent. In slow environments (CI), the 26 rapid updates in the test loop can take longer than the hard-coded 200ms delay to settle in the audit DB.

**Proposed Fix:** Instead of a static delayPromise(200), I plan to update the test to use a polling/retry mechanism (e.g., using a "wait-for" helper) that checks the audit DB until the history length matches the expected revCount % 10. This will make the test resilient to variable CI performance.

Hi @dianabarsan, @andrablaj 

I've analysed this failure, and I'd like to take this on.

**Analysis:** The 502 Bad Gateway from Nginx is likely a transient error caused by Nginx's DNS resolver cache (valid=10s). When the API restarts and potentially gets a new internal IP, Nginx may still attempt to connect to the old IP for a few seconds. While listenForApi() does poll for readiness, a subsequent request can still hit a race condition if Nginx's resolution state hasn't stabilised or if the network is briefly flaky.

**Proposed Fix:** Instead of patching only this specific test, I propose adding robust retry logic to the central request() helper in tests/utils/index.js. By allowing the utility to automatically retry (e.g., 3 times with a short backoff) specifically for 502 and 504 errors, we can stabilise this test and prevent similar "suspicious" failures across the entire integration suite.

Essentially the analyzer controls what tokens are "indexed" (and therefore are searchable).  You can use the [/_nouveau_analyze](https://docs.couchdb.org/en/stable/ddocs/nouveau.html#testing-analyzer-tokenization) Couch endpoint to see what tokens are emitted by different analyzers for some given input. - `keyword` - `१२३४६dfsd12346 हैलो सेटिङहरू`

Unfortunately, I have not found any analyzer that will emit tokens for both `12346` and  `१२३४६`. 🤔 With the `hindi` analyzer, it at least seems like we can be confident Devanagari numerals will be emitted as Arabic.  This could simplify our search handling logic a bit at least since it would mean that we would just need to have a one-way normalization of the search input to convert any Devanagari numerals in the search text to Arabic before submitting the search query (with the `whitespace` analyzer we would always need to search for _both_ the Devanagari and the Arabic). Hi @dianabarsan, @andrablaj 

I've analysed this issue and would like to work on a fix.

The crash is caused by a race condition in contacts-content.component.ts. When a user switches pages quickly, the Redux store clears the selectedContact, setting it to null. However, asynchronous callbacks from XmlFormsService or pending Redux emits still trigger updateFastActions() or setChildTypesBySelectedContact(), which attempt to read .doc on the now-null contact.

I plan to solve this by:

Adding null guards (optional chaining) to this.selectedContact throughout the component.

Implementing early returns in methods like updateFastActions and setChildTypesBySelectedContact if the contact has been cleared.

Adding checks within the XmlFormsService subscription callbacks to ensure they only execute if the component still has an active contact.

Could you please assign this to me? 

Thanks.

Update the mapping logic to correctly route uploaded files to the right sub-report doc. Unlike contacts, owner lookup is easier: each `[db-doc="true"]` element already has a `_couchId` set by `mapOrAssignId`, corresponding to the sub-doc's `_id`.

1. **Build a sub-doc lookup map** — sub-docs by `_id` <> prepared doc. 
2. **Resolve owner by nearest `[db-doc="true"]` ancestor** — walk up from the binary node; if any ancestor has a `_couchId` in the map, that sub-doc owns the attachment; otherwise fall back to the main doc.
3. **Route file-widget uploads** — for each `File` from `FileManager.getCurrentFiles()`, find the `[type=binary]` node whose text content equals `file.name` (filenames are globally unique within a form session — timestamp is appended) , resolve its owner, attach there.
4. **Do the same for inline binary blobs** — for each non-empty `[type=binary]` node, resolve its owner and attach the base64 content there

I think these are detecting a race condition in the code, not just the tests.

after transitions are applied to a document, the list of transitions that have run is added to the infodoc.
https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/8c0cefbd0bafefffecc2a4cb9f8ca29f703db491/shared-libs/transitions/src/transitions/index.js#L260
the modified document is saved, and if successful, the infodoc with the updated list of transitions is saved.

Subsequent changes to the document don't run the same transitions, because all transitions have a hasRun filter that checks the infoDoc to see if it has already run.
e.g. https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/8c0cefbd0bafefffecc2a4cb9f8ca29f703db491/shared-libs/transitions/src/transitions/death_reporting.js#L58 . this is specific to death_reporting, but there are similar checks in all transitions.
https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/8c0cefbd0bafefffecc2a4cb9f8ca29f703db491/shared-libs/transitions/src/transitions/utils.js#L72

The api runs some transitions synchronously, before documents are saved, without triggering sentinel.
This leads to a race condition where

1. api saves the document after applying transitions.
2. sentinel gets the changed document from the changes feed
3. sentinel gets the infodoc for the change; but the transitions list hasn't been updated yet
4. sentinel runs the same transitions as api (duplicates) because it doesn't know they were already run
5. api saves the infodoc with the updated transitions, but sentinel has already run.

I didn't come up with a way to reproduce this reliably without changing the code, but adding a delay at https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/8c0cefbd0bafefffecc2a4cb9f8ca29f703db491/shared-libs/transitions/src/transitions/index.js#L269 to allow sentinel to run before the infodoc is saved causes these tests to fail reliably

I think that the only reliable way to resolve this is to save the infodoc before the medic doc. 
But that's with a big caveat, because in case the medic doc save fails we would need to revert the infodoc, and that can lead to all manner of weird timing inconsistencies (maybe we'd just be creating MORE race conditions). 

Or, we somehow "lock" the infodoc, this means that there are two writes happening to the infodoc. 
Off the top of my head, I would "lock" the infodoc, writing the _rev of the medic doc that we are running transitions over, and then "unlock" it when done. Sentinel would not process a doc that is infodoc locked. 
A bit more involved, but it would save us from further race conditions.

Hello @dianabarsan 
After investigating the stack trace from #9993:

**Root cause:**
The crash at `te._destroy` inside PouchDB's IDB adapter occurs because `aggregateMapReduce(db)` calls `db.query()` which opens an IDB cursortransaction to iterate over telemetry documents. Although `awaitPromise.all([...aggregateMapReduce(db)...])` resolves at the JavaScript level, the underlying IDB transaction has not yet fullycommitted at the browser level. When `db.destroy()` is called immediately after, PouchDB tries to abort all open IDB transactionsand hits this still-committing cursor transaction, throwing:

"Failed to read the 'result' property from 'IDBRequest':The request has not finished."

The pending IDB requests are specifically the cursor transactionsopened by pouchdb-mapreduce's `db.query()` inside `aggregateMapReduce()`.

**Fix:**
`await db.close()` before `await db.destroy()` is the correct solution.PouchDB's `close()` waits for all pending IDB transactions to finish before closing the connection, which prevents `destroy()` from encountering the still-open cursor transaction.

Also keeping the `let db` fix which resolves the variable shadowing bug where the catch block was calling `closeDataBase(undefined)` instead ofthe actual db instance.

So I tried a couple of things.
Just saving the transitions before the medic documents, for both `processDocs` and `processChanges`, does lead to more race conditions which can be reliably reproduced in tests. Specifically, when saving messages, api tries to update a message while sentinel is running transitions, and sentinel gets a conflict when it also tries to save the message. Then the transitions don't ever re-run on the next change because infodoc says they already ran. Currently, there's no explict retry, but transitions do get rerun on the next change. Which may not be intentional ([this comment ](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/58547e47671d5c008852825ace505bafcf80bbc0/shared-libs/transitions/src/transitions/index.js#L261) suggests its not) but tests, and maybe even production code, rely on it.

I also tried saving the infodoc first, and if saving the medic document fails, rolling it back. There is still a possibility for inconsistent infodocs if the sentinel process stops after saving the infodoc but before saving the medic doc, or if the rollback itself fails. Maybe still a possibility but seems too complicated for not any real guarantees.

What I came up with is [saving the infodocs first in processDocs only](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/pull/10910), and for processChanges, keeping the current behavior of saving the transitions after saving the medic doc.
This sidesteps the race condition for transitions run by api by not triggering sentinel until after transitions are saved. It doesn't solve the other race condition where sentinel gets a conflict, but keeps the current behavior where transitions are rerun on the the next change.
Which gets the tests to pass, but is mediocre in several ways, and still allows the possibility for the infodoc to be inconsistent and show that transitions have run when the haven't. Maybe that doesn't really matter? if it did can detect this with last_rev; if `transitions.last_rev`  is the same as the current rev of the medic document, the the medic document wasn't saved. 

Locking the infodoc would be less janky, but by itself wouldn't solve this particular issue, unless we can change sentinel's behavior, or have sentinel wait for the lock somehow, instead of just not processing the change at all.
Sentinel still needs to run async transitions even if api ran 'sync' transitions.  "should run async and sync transitions over the same doc successfully" tests this directly https://github.com/medic/cht-core/blob/58547e47671d5c008852825ace505bafcf80bbc0/tests/integration/transitions/sentinel-api-transitions.spec.js#L852
So locking the infodoc, and having sentinel not process the doc at all if its infodoc was locked wouldn't allow that; it would need to wait until the lock was "released".

Hi @dianabarsan,

> Is there something in the CHT codebase that might be leaving an IDB request open after aggregate() resolves?

I don't believe there is anything of the sort. We actively try to not do any low-level actions that can have these kinds of obscure consequences. 

> Should I look at the PouchDB source for _destroy directly to understand what requests it encounters?

I think this would be the only way to fully understand this. 
I think we can't just accept that transactions just hang beyond what PouchDb reports as fulfilled, this would have severe consequences in how the adapter should be treated and would require changes upstream. And given that the aggregation function specifically does not allow parallel executions, and we can exclude weird scenarios where multiple tabs would be open (since this is an e2e test and we _know_ we are only running one test at a time).

> having both system process documents in parallel.

ideally both systems shouldn't need to process documents in parallel; api would run the sync transitions, then sentinel runs the async transitions afterwards. There's no reason for them to be processing the same document at the same time, except it being difficult to prevent for other reasons.

so locking is conceptually cleaner, but more complex and solves a concurrency problem that ideally wouldn't exist at all
reordering saves is simpler and solves the ordering issue directly, but is messier

the question is which we prefer

> That double-counted the rate limiter's own response.

Hi @officialasishkumar consuming on 429 is not really double counting; the intention is to keep rate limiting until the number of failed requests actually reduces; otherwise, rate limited clients will stop being rate limited because they are receiving 429 instead of 401, even if the number of requests doesn't actually reduce.

Which is not necessarily wrong either, they would get rate limited again if they kept sending requests in the next 10 second window. 

> When several clients share a single key (most importantly a single req.ip, because a reverse proxy is not forwarding the real client address), one badly behaved client can exhaust that shared key, after which every other caller gets 429 from the controller

The root cause is that clients should not share a single key if they are not actually the same client. I think would rather leave the existing behavior around 429s and fix the root cause (which could be [allowing opting out or using a forwarded IP](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues/10705#issuecomment-4333862957))

Hey team, I found this performance bottleneck while profiling the contact detail page rendering path.

The contact detail page is the most visited page in the CHT app, and it was doing repeated Array.find() scans inside loops when loading reports. With the 500 report limit and hundreds of child contacts at a facility, this created O(n * m) complexity that can reach ~250,000 comparisons on a single page load. On the low end Android devices that CHWs typically use, this kind of thing really adds up.

The fix is straightforward: pre-build Map objects for O(1) lookups instead of scanning arrays every iteration. This brings the complexity down to O(n + m) with no behavioral changes.

I also removed the lodash _find import since it was only used in getHeading() and native Map.get() is both faster and avoids the external dependency.

All existing unit tests pass without modification, which confirms there is no behavioral change, just a performance improvement.

Hi @sugat009 @jkuester,
Pretty interested in this one. Spent a few hours going through the issue and reading `cht-conf/src/fn/{move,merge,delete}-contacts.js` along with the `HierarchyOperations` lib they all call into. Wanted to share my plan before going deeper a couple of the choices feel like things I shouldn't decide on my own.

## How I'd actually build it
Ship them one at a time in this order: delete → move → merge. That also happens to be roughly the order of how hard they are.

- Delete is mostly a recursive bulk-delete on the subtree.
- Move adds the lineage rewrite across all the descendants and their linked reports and tasks.
- Merge sits on top of all that and adds field-level conflict resolution plus reassigning every linked doc to the survivor.

_For each endpoint I'd add:_
- A controller in `api/src/controllers/` matching the shape of the existing person and place ones.
- Route and permission middleware using the `hasAny(['can_delete_contacts', 'can_edit'])` pattern from the issue.
- Unit tests on the controller plus integration tests against a real CouchDB (the Docker setup already supports that).

The midpoint milestone (delete and move both done with tests) feels realistic on this plan. Merge will be the slow one, mostly because of the conflict semantics rather than the code itself.

## Something I want to flag early
The cht-conf CLI files are basically thin wrappers `move-contacts.js` is around 70 lines and all the actual work happens inside `HierarchyOperations`. So we have a choice.

1. Port that logic into cht-core, or
2. Extract it into a shared package that both repos depend on.

My gut says port-and-eventually-deprecate is cleaner long term, but I don't want to lock that in without checking with you first.

## Two things I'd really like your input on
### 1. Sync response vs. background job with polling - how big do you want this to get?
The issue itself flags this as a TODO and honestly it's the biggest call to make on this whole project. A synchronous v1 is way simpler and probably fine for most hierarchies in practice. The polling pattern is the right answer eventually, but it brings a lot of new stuff with it: a persistent job table, a status endpoint, retention and cleanup policy, a worker model.
Do you have any numbers on the p95 subtree size for these operations in production? If most moves finish in under ~30 seconds, I'd push for sync first with a documented timeout, and layer in `/api/v1/operation` once we actually see real cases hitting the wall. But if the data says otherwise, I'd rather know now and budget for the bigger build from week 1.

### 2. How do we want to handle partial failures, given CouchDB has no multi-doc transactions?
A move on a deep subtree can easily touch thousands of docs across multiple `_bulk_docs` calls. If the API process dies halfway, or a batch hits a `409` storm, we end up with some descendants re-parented and some not and a naive retry would then double-rewrite the lineage of the ones that already moved.
cht-conf sidesteps this by staging the whole changeset as JSON files for the operator to review and upload, which works for a CLI but doesn't really translate to a single REST call. Would you be open to a plan-then-apply approach internally, where the server computes the full change set first, persists it (something like a `_local` doc or a job record), then applies in resumable batches? Or is there already a primitive in cht-core for this that I should be reusing instead of inventing something new?

Happy to prototype in either direction. Just want to make sure I'm not solving the wrong problem before I commit to it. 
Thanks!

@Vedd-Patel I am not super confident that we are "design complete" on this issue yet. 😬 There are still some open questions and I am worried about more unknown unknowns.  

That being said, if you are interested in building a prototype for a "Switch User" workflow, I think that would be a useful next step here!  Basically what I am thinking of is supporting something similar to the way on Gmail (and other Google properties) you can be logged into multiple Google accounts at the same and you can switch between accounts without having to logout/login each time.  The basic flow would be like:

- User is logged in
- From the sidebar menu, the user can choose to "Log out" or to "Switch user".
- Selecting "Switch user" takes them to a page where they can choose from a list of users with current sessions on the device or they can "Add account"
    - Selecting a user from the list should take them back to the app logged in as that user. They should not be prompted to re-authenticate.  Selecting a different existing account on the device should work even when the device is offline and does not have a connection to the server.
    - Selecting "Add account" should take them to the login page where they can authenticate as a new user on the device.  As normal, the login page should only work when the device is online and has a connection to the server.
- In either case, their original user session cookie should not be removed from the device. If they again select "Switch user", they should see both their current and the original user in the list of accounts they can choose.  

Regarding switching users offline, the _data_ for the different users is already stored separately in the browser storage.  Because the CHT is offline-first, when a user logs in on a new device, we download all the necessary data for the user to the device.  When a user logs out, their session cookie is cleared, but their data remains cached on the device such that it is keyed specifically to the user. When a different user logs in on the same device the original user's data is not replaced, but exists totally separated from the new users data.  This is all good news for us here because I think it means that we do not need to worry too much about the _data storage_ side of things. That might just work. 🤷 

The primary thing we will need to figure out is how to cache/swap session cookies when switching between users... 👍 

Anyway, like I mentioned at the start, it is probably best if we don't immediately try for a "ready to merge" PR here. But a working prototype branch would be a great way to continue pushing this feature forwards!

Hi @dianabarsan and @andrablaj, I'd like to take on fixing this.

**Root cause:** When editing a report, the form is prepopulated from `doc.fields` (a JSON object). Since this doesn't contain the original `<_id>` values nested inside `db-doc` elements, `xmlToDocs()` in `enketo.service.ts` generates brand-new UUIDs for each `db-doc=true` element on every save. The old extra docs in CouchDB are never cleaned up, so every edit creates fresh duplicates alongside the originals.

**Proposed fix: Option 2** — skip creating extra docs when editing an existing report.

The detection is simple: when editing, the doc fetched via `update()` has a `_rev` field; a new submission created via `create()` does not. Using `const isEdit = !!doc._rev` inside `xmlToDocs()`, we can:
* Still collect `db-doc` tag names (so `hidden_fields` stays correct on the edited report).
* Skip the `db-doc-ref` ID-overwriting step (so existing cross-reference values from `doc.fields` are preserved as-is).
* Return an empty extra-docs array, leaving the original extra docs in CouchDB untouched.

This means `db-doc` section data the user edits still flows into `doc.fields` of the report (visible and updated), but no new CouchDB documents are created and the old ones aren't touched — fixing the duplication without any risk of data loss.

I am aware this introduces a minor "Data Desync" trade-off (e.g., editing a name in the report won't update the associated extra doc). However, as Diana noted, attempting to update existing docs (Option 5) is highly dangerous and risks overwriting external changes. Options 3/4 require more invasive UI changes and are better suited as follow-ups if needed. Option 2 is the safest minimal fix that unblocks affected projects while prioritizing data integrity.

Happy to hear any concerns or suggestions. If this sounds good, I'll go for implementation.

Hey @dianabarsan, I looked into this.

It looks like the issue is happening because purged docs get saved as stubs (_deleted: true). Since change.doc ends up undefined, the Rules Engine filter just silently drops them, meaning those contacts never get marked as dirty.

I was thinking we could fix this by grabbing the full doc right before the purge actually happens. We could do a quick allDocs fetch in getDeletesAndPurges right before the bulkDocs call, and then pass those docs over to a new method in the rules engine to extract the subject IDs and trigger the recalculations.

This way, we handle it exactly like normal live deletions without having to touch the main changes feed filter. Does this approach sound good to you? Happy to give hand on this.

Hi @jkuester @binokaryg — I've opened PR #11044 implementing the index-time + query-time normalization approach you described.

**What it does:**
- Adds a `normalizeNumerals()` function in each of the 3 offline freetext views and 2 Nouveau index files, converting Devanagari digits (U+0966–U+096F) to Latin digits before emitting/indexing — so only `12345` is ever stored, never `१२३४५`
- Normalizes the same way in `normalizeFreetextQualifier()` in `cht-datasource/src/local/libs/core.ts`, so both online and offline queries always use Latin digits

This gives the full cross-matching matrix (Latin query → Devanagari result and vice versa) for both online (Nouveau) and offline (PouchDB) users, without touching analyzers.

Unit tests are included for all three offline view specs and `core.spec.ts`. E2E tests are flagged in the PR checklist as a follow-up.

Happy to incorporate any feedback!

HI @jkuester, @andrablaj

I've analysed this issue and can confirm it still exists in the current codebase (v5.1.0).

The root cause is that the `onMatch` function in` accept_case_reports.js` returns the result of `silenceRegistrations(...)`, which resolves to `undefined`. In the CHT transition framework, `onMatch` must resolve to a truthy value (like `true`) to signal that the document has been modified and should be persisted. Because it currently resolves to `undefined`, the updates (like setting `place_uuid`) are never saved to the database.

I noticed that other similar transitions like `accept_patient_reports.js` and `registration.js` have already been fixed by adding `.then(() => true)`, but this was missed for `accept_case_reports.js`.

I would like to fix this and add a regression test to ensure `onMatch` returns the correct truthy value.

@dianabarsan Here is the performance comparison across the requested data sizes.

### Benchmark setup

Isolated microbenchmark simulating the two hot paths changed in this PR:
1. **`addHeading`**: matching summaries to reports (by `_id`) and reports to forms (by `code`)
2. **`getReports`**: matching reports to contacts (by `patient_id`)

Each measurement: 10,000 iterations at the given report count.

### Results: `addHeading` — Array.find vs Map.get

| Reports | Array.find (ms) | Map.get (ms) | Speedup |
|---------|-----------------|--------------|---------|
| 10      | 54.58           | 23.92        | 2.3x    |
| 50      | 240.57          | 62.16        | 3.9x    |
| 100     | 356.84          | 104.28       | 3.4x    |
| 250     | 1,610.13        | 252.53       | 6.4x    |
| 500     | 8,316.57        | 533.44       | 15.6x   |

### Results: `getReports` — Array.find vs Map.get

| Reports | Array.find (ms) | Map.get (ms) | Speedup |
|---------|-----------------|--------------|---------|
| 10      | 15.63           | 14.42        | 1.1x    |
| 50      | 99.27           | 43.48        | 2.3x    |
| 100     | 211.12          | 70.34        | 3.0x    |
| 250     | 296.22          | 124.22       | 2.4x    |
| 500     | 497.73          | 213.32       | 2.3x    |

### Key observations

- At **realistic page sizes (10-50 reports)**, the improvement is modest but consistent (2-4x for `addHeading`, 1-2x for `getReports`).

based on your explanation and the `shift-based shared device` threat model, here is my proposed technical approach for the "Switch User" prototype:

### 1. UI workflow updates
* **sidebar menu:** add a new `Switch User` button alongside the existing `Log out` option
* **account selector view:** create a new angular route/component that acts as the account switcher hub
    * it will display a list of all locally cached accounts (usernames/profiles)
    * it will include an `Add account` button that redirects to the standard online login flow
* **no auth on switch (for now):** as per the current prototype scope, selecting an existing user from the list will immediately load their data without requiring a pin/password

### 2. session management 
since CHT already isolates IndexedDB/PouchDB data by user, the primary technical challenge is managing the authentication state and session cookies

**proposed mechanism:**
when a user clicks "Switch User":
1.  **cache the session:** we intercept the standard logout flow, instead of clearing the session cookie and destroying the token, we extract the active session token/cookie and store it locally (ex, in a secure `localStorage` array or dedicated IndexedDB table) keyed to that specific username
2.  **clear active session:** we clear the *active* browser session cookie so the app registers a logged-out state, routing the user to the account selector view
3.  **restore session (offline swapping):** when the user clicks an existing profile from the account selector view, we retrieve their previously cached session token, write it back to the active browser session, and trigger the standard app initialization flow 

since the CHT app checks for an active session to grant access to the locally cached PouchDB data, swapping the local token allows us to bypass the network authentication requirement entirely for offline switching

### 3. next steps

Hey @jkuester @mrjones-plip, I spent some time looking at the complexity concerns that led to closing this, and I think there’s actually a clean way to solve them.

The sticking point in Wrapper Auth was always the stateful mapping between OAuth tokens and CouchDB sessions, you'd need a cache, maintenance overhead, the whole thing. But if the access token is a **stateless JWT** signed with CouchDB's own `couch_httpd_auth/secret` (which `sso-login.js` already reads), that mapping disappears entirely. Every Bearer token request validates locally via HMAC —> no DB roundtrip, no cache.

On the CouchDB side, nothing changes. This is explicitly not Circular Auth, we're not reconfiguring Couch to accept JWTs. The API validates the token, sets `req.userCtx`, and the rest of the existing auth middleware runs exactly as-is. Cookie and Basic auth paths are untouched too.

Concretely it's about 5 files: a new service for client registration + JWT sign/verify, a controller for the authorize/token endpoints, a consent page template, one new branch in `auth.getUserCtx`, and route registrations. Auth codes get deleted on use so CouchDB's MVCC handles concurrent replay natively —> no soft-delete flag, no race condition.

MVP scope would be Authorization Code flow only (confidential clients), single `cht` scope that just inherits the user's existing roles, and an admin API for registering clients. No refresh tokens, no PKCE, no introspection —> all explicitly deferred.

Most of the blocking issues shared a root                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    
  cause in the old rolling-doc + periodic-save design; rewrote that core                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
  instead of patching each symptom.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                
  ## Architecture rewrite (covers blocking #2, #3, #5, #7)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
                                                                        
  Events are buffered in memory and persisted in batches to a per-day local                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     
  PouchDB (`interaction-YYYY-M-D-{user}`). On each app `init()`, any per-day
  DB that isn't "today" is aggregated into a single `interaction-log` doc in                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    
  the user's meta DB and the source DB is destroyed.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                
  - No periodic `save()` timer → no cap-halving double-count.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
  - No shared rolling doc → no `_persist` race; writes are append-only  
    `bulkDocs` to per-day DBs, aggregation is serialized by an                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
    `aggregationInFlight` promise guard.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
  - Day-rollover handled in `record()` via `rolloverAndCheckCapacity`, which                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    
    flushes the buffer and resets `persistedEventCount` — fixes the day N+1                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     
    block.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
  - `getServiceWorker()` is called once per stale per-day DB during init,                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       
    not on every persist. Down from ~96/shift to 0–1.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           
  - `this.user` is captured in `init()`; aggregate `_id` includes                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               
    `(date, user, deviceId)`. No user-context drift between record and                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          
    persist.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    
  - Aggregate is only written when `init()` finds a real `userCtx().name`,
    so `metadata.user` never falls back to `'unknown'`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                        
  ## Direct fixes from the review                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               
                                                                        
  - Registered `can_track_task_interactions` in                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 
    `config/default/app_settings.json` (#6).                            
  - Added `interaction-` to `webapp/src/js/bootstrapper/purger.js` prefix
    filter so IDB cleans up on the webapp side too (#4).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
  - Removed the unreliable `beforeunload` flush; only `visibilitychange`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
    triggers `persistBuffer()`.

    `initRulesEngine`, so by the time `/tasks` is reachable, init has

Hey @mrjones-plip, I've been digging through the codebase a bit and wanted to chime in on some of the open questions with things I found that might help shape the approach.

The good news is that the hardest part (collecting the data) is already done. The `GET /api/v1/impact` endpoint shipped in 5.0 already returns user counts, contact counts by type, and report counts by form, all pre-aggregated and anonymous. So the periodic reporting layer would essentially just be a scheduler that calls that existing service and POSTs the result to a central endpoint. Not a lot of net-new logic.

On **CI spam**, the simplest solution is checking `process.env.CI === "true"` before sending. GitHub Actions (and most other CI platforms) set this automatically, so there is no configuration burden on teams. As a secondary guard, CHT already uses `UNIT_TEST_ENV=1` throughout the codebase to short-circuit external calls in tests, so we could honour that too.

For **dev/TDG spam**, the `@medic/environment` shared lib already exposes `environment.host`, and `@medic/couch-request` even has an `isInternalRequest()` helper that checks if a URL targets that host. We could reuse that same pattern to simply refuse to send if the instance is running on `localhost` or `127.0.0.1`. Covers the "developer smashes 100k pregnancies into their local instance" scenario without any manual config.

On the **configurable endpoint** question, I'd lean towards putting it in `app_settings.json` rather than an environment variable, something like:

```json
"impact_reporting": {
  "enabled": false,
  "endpoint": "https://impact.medicmobile.org/api/v1/metrics",
  "interval_days": 7
}
```

This way large national deployments or Ministries of Health can point to their own ingestion server through the normal cht-conf/admin panel workflow, no server access needed. It also means changes pick up at runtime via the config watcher without restarting the API.

On **instance identity**, I think the opaque UUID approach is the right call. CHT now requires Node 22, which ships `crypto.randomUUID()` natively with no extra dependency. Generate it on first run, store it in CouchDB, include it with every payload. The central server gets something it can deduplicate and rate-limit against, but it cannot tie the UUID back to a specific partner without a separate out-of-band mapping. The key is making that tradeoff crystal clear in the opt-in prompt.

For **where the scheduler lives**, Sentinel's `schedule/` directory already has a clean pattern for exactly this kind of periodic background task. The purging job reads a cron expression from `app_settings`, parses it with `later.js`, and fires via `setTimeout` at the next scheduled time. We would follow the same pattern for an `impact-reporting.js` task, storing a `last_sent_at` timestamp in CouchDB to decide whether the interval has elapsed.

And for the **cht-conf opt-in flow**, `src/lib/user-prompt.js` already handles interactive CLI prompts via `readline-sync`. A new `configure-impact-reporting` action could walk the admin through what data is shared, get their explicit yes/no, and push the updated `impact_reporting.enabled` flag to the instance, keeping the consent moment admin-driven and auditable.

Given the goal is making `docker-helper` scripting-friendly (especially to fix the `stdin.write('y\n')` workaround currently used in the `cht-conf` E2E tests in medic/cht-conf#620), I propose we start with the first option: **Adding support for passing arguments/flags to bypass the interactive prompts.** Rather than a full JavaScript rewrite, we can keep the existing bash script but add standard POSIX flag parsing using a standard `while`/`shift` loop.

For example, a CI script could run:
`./scripts/docker-helper.sh --project-name myproject --cht-version 4.5.0`

If `--project-name` (or `-n`) is passed, it skips the interactive `select`/`read` prompts and creates/starts the project using the provided flags (falling back to defaults for any missing flags). If no flags are passed, the script behaves exactly as it does today with the interactive menu. Existing positional arguments (`./script myproject.env stop`) would remain unchanged.

I think you have pretty clearly understood my PR. :+1:  Just a couple comments:

> Approach A: standardize as much as possible with [type=file] approach by populating the type=binary field value with the attachment name. 

I 100% was hoping this would work out as you have described. :sweat: Unfortunately, it did not really seem to save us any complexity. 

> This saves us the extra logic of constructing base64 string from the attachment for edit. The report view is handled by reading the attachment directly and injecting it as an image like any other file object of type image. 

The `format-data-record` service will still need to keep the extra logic to support any existing reports with the `user-file/` format.  And the logic in the `reports-add` component for loading the image attachments when editing a report will still not work for `type=binary` fields (because the form model knows that they are not `type=file` fields and so their handling logic is totally different).

On top of that, changing to store the attachment name as the property value for `type=binary` fields ends up creating new challenges _in the edit workflow:_

1. If we do not do anything and just leave the attachment name set as the value, it breaks the `display-base64-image` preview functionality so that a "invalid image" icon is shown in the form (instead of the current edit "functionality" where _nothing_ is shown when editing a report for the `display-base64-image` fields.... :grimacing: (FTR, we can avoid the icon and actually display the image if we re-load the base64 data from the attachment back into the property value before rendering the form. However, as I found in my first commit, this is not super easy. We will probably need to support this eventually, though... :shrug: )
2. If/when we end up re-injecting the base64 image data for `type=binary` fields on edit, we immediately hit the challenge of how to avoid adding a duplicate attachment file each time the report is edited even if the `type=binary` field did not change.  Using a random uuid-based attachment name is obviously a problem because we would always get different names. My first commit used the hash of the file contents which worked but added overhead/complexity. Another option would be to just use the path to the field (e.g. like the original `type=binary` logic was doing).  

It ended up being similar complexity to just properly calculate the field path (even for the sub-docs).  That was the point where I started trying to figure out what benefits I was actually getting from `Approach A.`

On the other hand, with `Approach B.`, we end up with a minimal amount of code changed and all the `type=binary` logic still just follows what it was doing before (but now also works for sub-docs).  We have not simplified anything, but we really have not _added_ much more complexity either... :sweat_smile: :shrug: 

---

@benkags if you have a strong preference for `Approach A`, I am not set against it (as long as we can find a maintainable way to sort out the above challenges).  Otherwise, I do think `Approach B` (as drafted in my PR) should result in the functionality we need with the minimal amount of changes.

Also happy to jump on a call to discuss further if that would be helpful!  :+1:

@andrablaj  While working on the purging module, I noticed that getRoles() at sentinel/src/lib/purging.js:69 loads every document from the _users database in a single allDocs({ include_docs: true }) call with no limit parameter. This is inconsistent with the rest of the purging module, which carefully paginates large queries  (e.g., batchedContactsPurge and purgeUnallocatedRecords both use batch limits and cursor-based iteration). In deployments with thousands of CHWs, this unbounded query creates an unnecessary memory spike on every purging cycle. I have submitted #11089 which paginates the query in batches of 1000, following the same   pattern used elsewhere in the file.

@andrablaj  While investigating the rate limiter behavior reported in #10705, I noticed a separate vector in the same getKeys() function at   api/src/services/rate-limit.js:29-31,36-38. The raw password is included as a rate limit key alongside IP and username. This means every login attempt sharing  the same password shares a single rate limit bucket. In CHT deployments where administrators provision passwords for community health workers, an attacker who uesses a commonly used password can exhaust the rate limit for that key and lock out every account using it, without ever knowing a valid username. Removing  the password from the key set leaves IP + username, which is sufficient to prevent brute-force attacks against individual accounts. I have submitted #11091 with the fix and updated tests.
